source.title_on_document: Large Language Model in Ideation for Product Innovation: An Exploratory Comparative Study

supplement.where: Appendix A (Mediation Tables A1-A5), printed on pp. 33-37 of this PDF and cited on p. 20 ('Appendix A shows the detailed results'). The document cites no separate or online supplement, data, or code.
supplement.holds: Mediation models for the five outcome variables (A1 Productivity, A2 Efficiency, A3 Idea Novelty, A4 Functional Appropriateness, A5 Divergent Thinking), each with the ChatGPT dummy and one process variable (Information Volume, Relatedness, Divergency, or Adoption): coefficients, SEs, p-values, and 95% bias-corrected CIs. The models' sample sizes are not printed. The ChatGPT coefficients there are direct effects conditional on a post-treatment mediator, not the arm contrast. No arm-level SD, and no SE for any arm difference, is printed anywhere in the document; Table 3 (pp. 19-20) gives arm means, ns, differences, and ANOVA F-statistics.

paper_design_summary: One hundred MTurk workers were randomly assigned to generate up to five new product ideas for coffee mugs with either an embedded ChatGPT panel (GPT-3.5-turbo via the OpenAI API) or an embedded Google Search panel (Custom Search JSON API); 90 were analyzed after 10 attention-check exclusions (45 per arm). Ideas were screened for validity, summarized by ChatGPT to at most 10 words, rated by MTurk raters for novelty and functional appropriateness, and scored for semantic divergence from the other ideas in the same condition with text embeddings; the number of valid ideas and valid ideas per second were also compared. Arms were compared by one-way ANOVA on participant-level scores.

studies.label: Online experiment: coffee-mug idea generation with ChatGPT vs Google Search

assignment.what_was_assigned: Ideation tool embedded in the task interface: an LLM chat assistant (ChatGPT, GPT-3.5-turbo) or a Google search engine
assignment.quote: Our study employs a between-subjects design consisting of two conditions: LLM and search engine. Participants were randomly assigned to one condition to generate innovative ideas for coffee mugs
assignment.locator: p. 9, Section 4 (Experimental Setup); also p. 11, Section 4, and p. 23, Section 6.2.2 ('random assignment at the participant level')

arms.name: LLM (ChatGPT)
arms.description: Custom interface: task description and five idea boxes on the left, an 'AI Assistant' chat panel on the right that called OpenAI's Chat Completion API with GPT-3.5-turbo, kept memory of recent prompts and responses, and had a 'Start a New Conversation' button. Participants were told to use only the assigned tool and to stay on the interface.

arms.name: Search Engine (Google Search)
arms.description: Same interface with a search panel on the right that used Google's Custom Search JSON API; participants could page through results and open result websites inside the panel.

participants.exclusions: 100 MTurk workers participated and were randomly assigned; 10 who failed attention checks in the post-task questionnaire were removed, leaving 90 analyzed participants (45 per arm; p. 11, Section 4; Table 1, p. 12). The per-arm split of the 100 randomized participants and of the 10 removed is not stated. Table 3 Panel C (p. 20) reports 67 analyzed participants for Idea Novelty, Functional Appropriateness, and Divergent Thinking (39 LLM, 28 Search Engine), matching those with at least one valid idea (p. 12, Section 5.1). Selection on valid ideas occurs after assignment and differs by arm. The divergence missingness sentence on p. 17 conflicts with these counts and remains unresolved. 64 of the 90 analyzed participants used the tools in the interface (32 per arm, Table 3 Panel A, p. 19), and 49 both used the tools and submitted a valid idea (Table 3 note, p. 20).
participants.who: MTurk workers with more than 5,000 approved tasks and an approval rate of at least 99%; paid US$1.50; IP addresses checked and no duplicates found
participants.quote: One hundred MTurk workers participated in the experiment. ... Ten participants who failed attention checks were removed. Our final sample comprised 90 participants, with 45 for each tool.
participants.locator: p. 11, Section 4; Table 1, p. 12; p. 12, Section 5.1; p. 20, Table 3 note

ai_tool.name_model: ChatGPT via OpenAI's Chat Completion API, GPT-3.5-turbo model, in a custom interface
ai_tool.how_used: Free prompting of an 'AI Assistant' panel beside the idea-submission form; participants could build on the conversation or start a new one. In a training task they had to send at least one message before reaching the task page. All prompts, responses, and the time on the interface were logged. Participants were told to use only the assigned tool and stay on the interface.

task.description: Come up with novel ideas for coffee mugs: up to five ideas, one per box, each a brief description of up to 500 characters, with no justification required (p. 9, Section 4; p. 10, Figure 2).
task.duration: not_stated (time on the interface was recorded and used for Efficiency; no time limit or mean duration is printed)

outcomes.name: Idea Novelty
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: MTurk raters (300 recruited; idea generators and attention-check failures excluded) each rated six randomly selected ideas on novel, original, and exciting (7-point Likert); each idea had 10.6 raters on average. Scores were z-normalized within rater, averaged over the three items per idea, then averaged over the participant's valid ideas. Raters saw ChatGPT (GPT-3.5-turbo) summaries of at most 10 words, which two postgraduate students checked against the originals. 228 of the 450 submitted ideas were valid (159 LLM, 69 Search Engine). Analyzed participants: 67 with at least one valid idea (39 LLM, 28 Search Engine).

contrasts.reported: Table 3 Panel C: LLM 0.010 (39) vs Search Engine -0.057 (28); Difference 0.018 (as printed; the two arm means differ by 0.067); F-statistic 4.88** (one-way ANOVA). Text p. 19: 'Idea Novelty: 0.010 vs. -0.057, p < 0.05'. No arm SDs. Table 2 (pooled, p. 17): Obs 67, mean 0.121, median 0.091, STD 0.209; this row may be swapped with the Functional Appropriateness row (see open_questions). Not the arm contrast: Table A3 ChatGPT coefficient conditional on one mediator, .1415462 (SE .0472364, p 0.004) with Information Volume; .0783577 (SE .0328887, p 0.021) with Information Adoption.
contrasts.locator: p. 20, Table 3 Panel C; p. 19 text; p. 17, Table 2; p. 35, Table A3

outcomes.name: Divergent Thinking (semantic divergence of ideas within condition)
outcomes.question: across_people
outcomes.measure_detail: For each idea, 1 minus the average cosine similarity between its embedding and the embeddings of all other ideas from participants in the same condition; the participant's score is the average over their ideas. Higher = more divergent. Embeddings from OpenAI text-embedding-ada-002, computed on the ChatGPT 10-word summaries; TF-IDF embeddings are said to give consistent results (footnote 10, not tabulated). The paper calls this measure 'Divergent Thinking'. Analyzed participants: 67 with at least one valid idea (39 LLM, 28 Search Engine).

contrasts.reported: Table 3 Panel C: LLM 0.134 (39) vs Search Engine 0.123 (28); Difference 0.011; F-statistic 25.68*** (one-way ANOVA). Text p. 19: 'participants in the LLM condition generated more diverse ideas than those in the Search Engine condition (0.134 vs. 0.123, p < 0.01)'. Higher = more divergent, so no sign reversal. No arm SDs. Table 2's Divergent Thinking row (Obs 67, mean -0.018, median -0.008, STD 0.126) repeats the Functional Appropriateness row, so no valid pooled SD is printed. Not the arm contrast: Table A5 ChatGPT coefficient conditional on one mediator, .0107992 (SE .0038407, p 0.007) with Information Volume.
contrasts.locator: p. 20, Table 3 Panel C; p. 19 text; p. 17, Table 2; p. 37, Table A5

diversity_detail.metric: Idea divergence = 1 minus the mean cosine similarity of an idea's embedding to the embeddings of all other ideas from participants in the same condition, averaged per participant (higher = more diverse)
diversity_detail.embedding_model: OpenAI text-embedding-ada-002 (TF-IDF as robustness, not tabulated)
diversity_detail.computed_over: Each idea against all other ideas from participants within the same condition, separately in each arm. The text does not say whether the participant's own other ideas or invalid ideas enter the comparison set; the Table 3 counts (39, 28) match the participants with at least one valid idea. The texts compared are the ChatGPT 10-word summaries.
diversity_detail.uncertainty: One-way ANOVA on participant-level averages (39 vs 28 participants); Table 3 prints an F-statistic with stars and no SE or CI for the arm difference. Appendix Table A5 gives SEs only for ChatGPT coefficients in models that also include a process variable; their sample sizes are not printed.
diversity_detail.notes: The comparison pools differ in size across arms (159 valid LLM ideas vs 69 Search Engine ideas). The p. 17 text says participants who did not use the tools have missing values, but Table 3's counts (39, 28) are the participants with a valid idea, not the tool users (32, 32). Table 2's Divergent Thinking row duplicates the Functional Appropriateness row.

outcomes.question: with_ai

All 90 analyzed participants submitted 5 ideas; 228 of the 450 were valid (159 LLM, 69 Search Engine). Analyzed participants: 90 (45 per arm).

company_involvement.description: No company authors, funding, or data provider stated: the authors are at HKUST and American University (p. 1), and the document has no funding or acknowledgment statement. The study used OpenAI's Chat Completion API and Google's Custom Search JSON API as tools (pp. 9-10).

eligibility.reason: Individual MTurk workers were randomly assigned to ChatGPT (GPT-3.5-turbo) or Google Search for coffee-mug idea generation (p. 9, Section 4; p. 11, recruitment; p. 23, Section 6.2.2). 100 were randomized and 90 analyzed (45 per arm) after 10 attention-check exclusions (p. 11; Table 1, p. 12). Table 3 Panel C reports 67 analyzed participants for novelty, functional appropriateness, and divergence (39 LLM, 28 Search Engine; p. 20), so even the rated-output comparisons exceed 50 people without counting ideas or raters. MTurk raters scored novelty and functional appropriateness on ChatGPT summaries of participants' submitted ideas (pp. 12-13, Section 5.1; p. 16, Section 5.2.3); semantic divergence was computed from idea embeddings (p. 17, Section 5.2.3 and footnote 10). AI was available during production in the ChatGPT arm (p. 9); the comparison is ai_vs_active. The numerical inconsistencies and uncertain divergence details affect extraction or interpretation, while the assignment, analyzed sample size, and output-based rating evidence independently establish all three eligibility criteria.

one_line_finding: Compared with participants assigned to Google Search, those assigned to ChatGPT submitted more valid ideas (3.533 vs 1.533, F = 27.65), ideas rated more novel (z-scores 0.010 vs -0.057, F = 4.88, p < 0.05) but less functionally appropriate (0.055 vs 0.213, F = 10.77, p < 0.01), and ideas more semantically divergent within their condition (0.134 vs 0.123, F = 25.68, p < 0.01) (Table 3, p. 20).
open_questions: Table 3 prints the Idea Novelty difference as 0.018, but the arm means 0.010 and -0.057 differ by 0.067; which figure is correct? The F-statistic (4.88) and the text's p < 0.05 do not settle it.

Table 2's Idea Novelty and Functional Appropriateness rows look swapped: the 39/28-weighted average of Table 3's Functional Appropriateness arm means is 0.121 (Table 2's Idea Novelty mean), and that of the Idea Novelty arm means is -0.018 (Table 2's Functional Appropriateness mean). If so, the pooled SD is 0.126 for Idea Novelty and 0.209 for Functional Appropriateness, the reverse of what is printed. Table 3, the p. 19 text, and the signs in Appendix Tables A3-A4 agree with one another.

Table 2's Divergent Thinking row repeats the Functional Appropriateness row (67, -0.018, -0.008, 0.126, -0.102, 0.068), so no valid pooled SD for divergence is printed; arm means of 0.134 and 0.123 cannot average to -0.018.

Table 3 Panel C analyzes 67 participants for the rated and embedded outcomes (39 of 45 LLM vs 28 of 45 Search Engine), matching those with at least one valid idea (p. 12). This selection occurs after assignment and differs by arm; the main comparison does not address it. For divergence, the missingness sentence on p. 17 conflicts with the tabulated counts.

No arm SD and no SE for any unadjusted arm difference is printed (Table 3, pp. 19-20; Appendix A, pp. 33-37). The appendix SEs describe coefficients conditional on a process variable. Confirmed participant-level variability and suitable uncertainty remain needed for effect extraction; no effect size is calculated in this form.
The per-arm split of the 100 randomized participants and of the 10 attention-check exclusions is not stated.

The rating counts do not reconcile: p. 16 reports 300 workers recruited, six ideas rated per worker, and 10.6 raters per idea, while p. 12 reports 228 valid ideas. The final numbers of raters and ratings and the evaluated idea set need clarification.
notes: Single study. Outcome IDs follow screener A's order; B's S1-O2 (Functional Appropriateness), S1-O3 (Productivity), and S1-O4 (Divergent Thinking) are S1-O3, S1-O4, and S1-O2 here. The comparison arm is a search engine, so every contrast is ai_vs_active. All 90 analyzed participants submitted five ideas (450), of which 228 were valid. Only 64 of the 90 used the embedded tool on the interface (32 per arm, Table 3 Panel A) despite the training requirement to send at least one message or query; AI availability is coded yes because the ChatGPT panel sat beside the idea form for every LLM participant. Ideas were rewritten by ChatGPT into summaries of at most 10 words before rating and embedding, in both arms, so raters and embeddings scored the summaries, not the original texts. Productivity is capped at five ideas. Not coded as outcomes: the input and process variables (Exploration Depth, Exploration Breadth, Information Volume, Relatedness, Divergency), which describe prompts or tool content; Information Adoption (share of idea sentences copied from tool content; LLM 0.418 (39) vs 0.255 (28), F = 3.78*, Table 3 Panel B), which is computed on the ideas but measures copying, not creativity; the Appendix A mediation models; and Tables 4-5 (novelty and appropriateness regressed on Information Adoption, ChatGPT, and their interaction with controls and entropy balancing, n = 49), which are not arm contrasts. The paper calls itself exploratory and says Section 6.2 does no formal hypothesis testing (p. 20). Final review (2026-10-08): read the entire markdown conversion, including references and Appendix A, and checked the recorded statistics and eligibility passages against the PDF. The assignment, people, and outcome challenge files all contain empty problems arrays; final challenge-resolution counts therefore remain zero. The remaining source-reporting uncertainties and their resolution routes are listed in final.open_items. source.supplement already correctly identifies the included Appendix A; design_class remains online_rct for this original experiment.

open_items.item: open_questions[0]: Table 3 prints an Idea Novelty difference of 0.018 beside arm means 0.010 and -0.057 (p. 20). Author confirmation of the intended means and difference would settle this effect-extraction discrepancy; eligibility does not depend on the effect magnitude.

open_questions[1]: The Table 2 Idea Novelty and Functional Appropriateness rows may be reversed (p. 17, compared with Table 3, p. 20). Author confirmation of the row labels and pooled SDs is needed for extraction. Both outcomes remain confirmed ratings of submitted ideas.

open_questions[2]: Table 2 repeats the Functional Appropriateness statistics in the Divergent Thinking row (p. 17), conflicting with the positive divergence arm means in Table 3 (p. 20). Authors would need to provide corrected divergence summary statistics. The rated-output evidence independently establishes eligibility.

open_questions[3], selection on valid ideas: This is a confirmed analysis limitation (p. 12, Section 5.1; p. 16, Section 5.2.3; p. 20, Table 3 Panel C). Random assignment is explicit and 67 people are analyzed for the rated outcomes, so no further information is needed for the three screening criteria. This does not establish an intention-to-treat effect.

open_questions[4]: Arm SDs and unadjusted arm-difference SEs are absent; Appendix A supplies mediator-adjusted coefficients instead (pp. 19-20, Table 3; pp. 33-37, Tables A1-A5). Participant-level data with assignment labels would permit appropriate variability and uncertainty estimation. No data URL is stated. This concerns effect extraction and pooling.

open_questions[5]: The allocation of the 100 randomized participants and 10 attention-check exclusions across arms is unreported (p. 11, Section 4). Author-provided assignment and exclusion counts would settle it; the 90 analyzed participants, 45 per arm, and the 67-person rated-output comparisons are explicit.

open_questions[6]: The reported rater recruitment, workload, average raters per idea, and valid-idea total do not reconcile (p. 16, Idea Quality; p. 12, Section 5.1). Authors would need to confirm the final rater count, number of ratings, and evaluated idea set. Raters are excluded from the eligibility participant count, and output scoring is explicit.

open_questions[3] and S1-O2.diversity_detail.notes: The divergence definition says tool nonusers have missing scores (p. 17), whereas Table 3 reports 39 and 28 analyzed participants for divergence and 32 tool users per arm (pp. 19-20). Author confirmation of the actual divergence sample would settle this conflict. The separately documented rated outcomes already satisfy the sample-size and output criteria.

S1-O2.diversity_detail.computed_over: The divergence comparison set is described as all other ideas in the same condition, without explicitly stating how a participant's own other ideas or invalid ideas were treated (p. 17, Section 5.2.3). Author confirmation of the implemented comparison rule would settle it. Across-participant comparison and output scoring are explicit.
